facts.claim: At the Madrian–Shea firm, one-year 401(k) participation rose from 49 percent under opt-in to 86 percent under automatic enrollment.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the default converted nonresponse from nonparticipation into participation while preserving opt-out.
facts.commonError: The increase required a larger employer match.
facts.whyWrong: The economic terms were unchanged when the enrollment rule changed.

facts.claim: Save More Tomorrow participants increased average saving from 3.5 to 13.6 percent over four pay raises and roughly 40 months.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because contribution increases coincided with raises, so saving grew without a nominal drop in take-home pay.
facts.commonError: The plan demanded an immediate ten-percentage-point contribution increase.
facts.whyWrong: Escalation was staged across future raises.

facts.claim: Vanguard's 2018 sample covered 473 plans, 59 percent of which used automatic enrollment and averaged 93 percent participation.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because default enrollment reduces the active steps required across many workplaces.
facts.commonError: Automatic enrollment remained confined to the original field experiment.
facts.whyWrong: Large record-keeper data show broad employer adoption.

facts.claim: Automatic enrollment also anchors many workers on the plan's default contribution rate.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because inertia affects both whether employees participate and whether they change the preassigned percentage.
facts.commonError: Once enrolled, workers routinely optimize their contribution immediately.

facts.claim: Save More Tomorrow asks for a commitment before the future raise arrives.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because a calm advance decision captures the preference to save before present bias and loss aversion operate on current pay.
facts.commonError: Employees decide separately after every raise whether to increase saving.
facts.whyWrong: The schedule is chosen in advance and then continues automatically.

facts.claim: Tying escalation to a pay raise reduces the felt loss associated with higher saving.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because take-home pay can still rise even as a larger fraction goes to retirement.
facts.commonError: Loss aversion disappears whenever saving earns a positive return.
facts.whyWrong: The salient reference point is current take-home pay, not only future wealth.

facts.claim: A retirement default must specify both a contribution level and an investment allocation.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because automatic enrollment creates balances that require a destination even when the worker makes no fund choice.
facts.commonError: Enrollment can be automated while leaving investment entirely undefined.
facts.whyWrong: Contributions cannot enter the plan without being allocated.

facts.claim: A diversified, low-fee lifecycle fund is a defensible default for workers who do not manage a portfolio.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because diversification limits idiosyncratic risk while age-based allocation reduces the need for repeated rebalancing.
facts.commonError: The employer's own stock is the safest default because employees know the company.
facts.whyWrong: Employment income and retirement wealth would then share the same firm-specific risk.

facts.claim: Many employees in retirement-plan studies report that their current saving rate is too low.
facts.mechanism: This mechanism operates because the self-assessment supplies welfare evidence that a directional increase aligns with participants' own stated goals.
facts.commonError: Any nudge toward higher saving necessarily imposes the architect's personal preference.
facts.whyWrong: Employee reports and easy opt-out can ground the direction in chooser welfare.
